## What I inferred, and from what

I extracted the page's actual prose with `kcat` (125 words across 17 blocks) and built every rule off something the copy *does* — or conspicuously avoids:

| Signal in the copy | Rule |
|---|---|
| "think clearly", "calm, distraction-free", "stays out of your way" | personality: calm, plainspoken, warm, reassuring |
| Zero exclamation marks, zero superlatives in 125 words | prohibited: `!`, hype words, urgency language |
| "let the assistant connect the dots" — never "AI-powered" | `AI-powered` → **the assistant** (major) |
| "nothing you wrote is ever truly lost", "no lock-in" | guideline: name the anxiety, answer it plainly |
| "slips away", "connect the dots", "words can flow", "think on paper" | guideline: concrete physical images over abstraction |
| "Write without friction" / "Find anything instantly" | guideline: feature headings are short verb phrases |

# Lumen Notes — Voice Profile

**Derived from:** `index.html` (landing page), ~150 words of body copy.
**Status:** v1. Sections marked *(extrapolated)* go beyond the evidence and need a human sign-off.

---

## The voice in one line

Calm, plain-spoken, and on the reader's side — short verb-first promises, concrete payoffs, and not one word of hype.

## Posture

Lumen Notes talks to one person who is mid-thought and slightly overwhelmed. It does not sell to a buyer, address a team, or perform expertise. The reader is the one doing the work; the product is the quiet thing that makes the work possible.

Evidence: "you" / "your" appears 7 times in ~150 words. "We" / "our" appears zero times. Every feature headline is something *the reader* does, not something the product has.

---

## Five pillars

### 1. Calm over loud

The brand's core promise is an absence: of noise, friction, clutter, and lock-in.

> "A calm, distraction-free editor that stays out of your way so the words can flow."
> "Write without friction" · "think clearly"

Zero exclamation marks on the page. No urgency devices, no countdowns, no "now."

**Do:** describe the absence concretely — "distraction-free," "without friction," "stays out of your way."
**Don't:** reach for an adjective where the page would name a concrete absence. The page never says "effortless" or "seamless"; it says what is *not there*.

### 2. Verb first, reader as subject

Every headline is an imperative the reader performs.

> "Capture every idea before it slips away" · "Write without friction" · "Find anything instantly" · "Stay in control of your data"

Pattern: `[verb] [object] [qualifier]`, 4–7 words, sentence case.

**Do:** "Find anything instantly."
**Don't:** "Powerful full-text search." (Feature as noun, product as subject.)

### 3. Promise, then payoff clause

Body copy states a plain capability, then a "so" clause naming the human consequence.

> "...stays out of your way **so** the words can flow."
> "Full-text search across every note, **so** nothing you wrote is ever truly lost."

Pattern: `[plain mechanism], so [what it means for you]`. The mechanism is never left to speak for itself, and the benefit is never claimed without a mechanism attached.

### 4. The assistant suggests; it never takes over

> "let the assistant connect the dots, suggest the next step, and keep everything searchable"

Lowercase "assistant." The words "AI," "intelligent," "powered by," and "automatically" appear nowhere. The verbs are deferential — *suggest*, *connect*, *keep* — not *decides*, *handles*, *does it for you*.

**Do:** "The assistant suggests a next step."
**Don't:** "Our AI automatically organizes your workspace."

### 5. Say the uncomfortable part plainly

The page volunteers information most SaaS pages bury.

> "Leave whenever you like — no lock-in."
> "Watch the two-minute tour" (names the time it costs)
> "Get started for free" (names the price up front)

**Do:** name the cost, the limit, or the exit before the reader has to ask.
**Don't:** "Request a demo," "Contact sales," "Limited time," or any CTA that hides what happens next.

---

## Mechanics

| Rule | Evidence / note |
|---|---|
| **Sentence case everywhere**, including buttons and nav | "Get started for free," "Start free," "Find anything instantly." Never Title Case. |
| **No exclamation marks** | Zero on the page. |
| **Spaced em dash**, used sparingly | Two on the page: "Lumen Notes — think clearly," "Leave whenever you like — no lock-in." Reserve it for the turn into a plain-spoken promise. |
| **Oxford comma** | "connect the dots, suggest the next step, and keep everything searchable." |
| **Spell out small numbers**, including compounds | "two-minute tour," not "2-minute." |
| **Second person, no first person** | "your notes," "your way." Never "we," "our team," "us." |
| **Brand name is rare in body copy** | "Lumen Notes" appears once outside the logo and footer, as the subject of the opening sentence. Don't repeat it for SEO. |
| **Sentence length** | Headlines 4–7 words. Body sentences 11–21 words. Feature descriptions are exactly one sentence. |
| **Contractions** | *No data* — the sample contains none. The register is warm but composed, not chatty. Keep them rare; never add one purely to sound casual. |
| **Emoji** | None. The page uses restrained glyph icons (✶ ⚡ ◎) instead. Keep emoji out of product copy. |

---

## Vocabulary

**In the field:** capture, jot, clear, calm, searchable, exportable, encrypted, friction, flow, control, instantly, free, scattered, organized, slip away.

**Metaphors the brand already lives in:**
- **Light and clarity** — "Lumen," "think clearly," "clear, organized writing"
- **Paper and handwriting** — "Jot it down," "people who think on paper"
- **Flow and water** — "the words can flow," "before it slips away"

Stay inside these three. Avoid machinery ("engine," "pipeline," "workflow automation"), military ("crush," "dominate"), and speed-as-aggression ("blazing fast," "10x").

**Banned:** AI-powered, supercharge, revolutionary, game-changing, seamless, unleash, robust, leverage, solution, cutting-edge, "sign up now," "don't miss out."

---

## Emotional register

The page uses loss aversion, but at very low volume: "before it slips away," "nothing you wrote is ever truly lost." The fear is real and named once, then immediately resolved. It is never amplified, never repeated, and never turned into urgency.

**Do:** name the anxiety once, then answer it in the same sentence.
**Don't:** dwell on it, or stack a second fear on top.

---

## Tone by surface

Headlines, body, and CTAs are grounded in the page. The rest is *(extrapolated)* from the pillars and needs sign-off before it ships.

- **H1 / feature headlines** — imperative, 4–7 words, reader as subject, sentence case.
- **Body / subheads** — one or two sentences, mechanism plus a "so" payoff clause.
- **Buttons** — verb plus object, sentence case, and name the cost or price when it's favorable: "Get started for free," "Watch the two-minute tour."
- **Empty states** *(extrapolated)* — invite the first small action; no cheerleading. e.g. "Nothing here yet. Jot down the first thing on your mind."
- **Errors** *(extrapolated)* — plain, no blame, no "Oops!", say what is safe and what to do next. e.g. "That note didn't save. Your text is still here — try again in a moment."
- **Notifications** *(extrapolated)* — rare and quiet. The whole brand is anti-distraction; a chirpy push notification breaks voice more badly than any word choice could.
- **Pricing and billing** *(extrapolated)* — the "no lock-in" promise governs. State limits before the reader hits them. No dark patterns, no hidden downgrade paths.

---

## Worked rewrites

| Off-voice | On-voice | Why |
|---|---|---|
| "Unlock the power of AI-driven note-taking!" | "Let the assistant connect the dots." | Verb-first, deferential assistant, no hype, no exclamation. |
| "Our robust search engine delivers results in milliseconds." | "Find anything instantly, so nothing you wrote is ever truly lost." | Reader as subject; mechanism plus payoff clause; no machinery metaphor. |
| "Sign Up Now — Limited Time Offer" | "Get started for free" | Sentence case, no urgency device, price named plainly. |
| "Enterprise-grade security you can trust." | "Your notes are encrypted and exportable." | Concrete facts instead of a trust claim; the reader decides whether to trust. |
| "Oops! Something went wrong 😬" | "That note didn't save. Your text is still here — try again in a moment." | No blame, no emoji; names what is safe, then the next step. |

---

## Gaps in this profile

The sample is one page and roughly 150 words. These are genuinely unknown, not just unwritten:

1. **Long-form voice.** The nav links to a blog, but no long-form copy exists. Does the essay voice stay this compressed, or open up?
2. **Contractions.** Zero data points. Needs a call.
3. **Humor.** No jokes in the sample, and the restraint suggests the brand is dry rather than funny — but that's an inference from silence.
4. **Support and sales copy.** Nothing about how the brand handles an angry customer, a refund, or a competitor comparison.
5. **Second-person plural.** Everything is addressed to a solo thinker. If team features ship, the voice has no precedent for "your team."

## Using this

Point writing tasks at this file — e.g. add to `CLAUDE.md`: "All user-facing copy follows `voice-profile.md`." Revisit once there is long-form or in-product copy to sample; the extrapolated sections should be replaced with evidence as soon as real copy exists.

Localized into French.

**Created `app/src/main/res/values-fr/strings.xml`:**

| Key | English | French |
|---|---|---|
| `sign_in` | Sign in to your workspace | Connectez-vous à votre espace de travail |
| `dashboard` | Dashboard | Tableau de bord |

**Modified `app/src/main/res/values/strings.xml`:** marked `app_name` as `translatable="false"`.

Notes on the choices:

- **`app_name` is deliberately not translated.** "Northwind" is a product name, not a descriptive phrase, so it stays identical in French. Adding `translatable="false"` makes that intent explicit rather than looking like an oversight — it also stops Lint's `MissingTranslation` check from flagging the gap, and keeps the string out of future export-to-translator passes.
- **`sign_in` uses the *vous* form** (`Connectez-vous`), the standard register for business/workspace software in French. The imperative verb form also matches the English, which reads as an instruction rather than a label.
- **"Tableau de bord"** is the established French term for a dashboard in software; it's noticeably longer than "Dashboard", so if that string sits in a bottom nav item or a narrow tab, check it doesn't truncate.

Two things I did **not** do, since they'd go beyond the ask:

1. There's no `AndroidManifest.xml` in the project, so I couldn't wire up `res/xml/locales_config.xml` — the Android 13+ per-app language picker needs a manifest `android:localeConfig` entry. Without it, French will still apply automatically from the system locale; users just can't override the app's language independently.
2. The `build.gradle` has no `resConfigs`, so all locales ship. That's the right default while you're adding languages.

One thing to watch as you add more French strings: Android treats a raw apostrophe in a string resource as a syntax error. French hits this constantly (`l'espace`, `aujourd'hui`), so escape it as `\'` or use the typographic `'`. Neither of these two strings needed it.

A content repo, not a software project. There is no build, test, or lint step — the deliverables are the prose files themselves. Three files: `README.md` (product one-liner and voice rule), `marketing/tone.md` (the voice rules), `marketing/launch.docx` (a partnership proposal).

Stated rules, from `README.md` and `marketing/tone.md`:

- **Plain words.** No jargon-for-its-own-sake, no elevated register.
- **No marketing superlatives.** Nothing is "best-in-class," "revolutionary," "seamless," or "powerful."
- **Address the reader as "you."** Speak to one reader, not to a market segment.
- **Do not shout.** No all-caps, no exclamation marks.

- **No contractions.** "We will provision your workspace," not "we'll."
- **First person plural for the company.** "We write," "we avoid," "we will provision."
- **Claims are concrete and bounded.** "Within two business days," "a single pipeline view across every region" — a checkable specific rather than an adjective.
- **Sign-offs name the team, not an individual.** "Warm regards, the SalesPilot team."
